---
title: "Cholecystectomy Techniques and Postoperative Problems"
format: revealjs
---


## Overview

- One of the most frequently performed general surgery procedures in the US
- Over 500,000 performed annually
- Frequency due to high prevalence of gallbladder disease
- Advent of laparoscopic cholecystectomy in the 1980s led to rapid rise in numbers

---

## Overview: Benefits of Laparoscopy

- Reduced postoperative recovery
- Reduced pain
- Ability to perform as outpatient procedure
- Incidence of open cholecystectomy has steadily decreased

---

## Overview: Chapter Goals

- Address open cholecystectomy techniques (still used when laparoscopy is contraindicated)
- Discuss laparoscopic cholecystectomy techniques
- Strategies to prevent common bile duct injuries (CBDI)
- Alternative minimally invasive approaches
- Common complications

---

## Indications: Symptomatic Gallstones

- Primary reason for cholecystectomy
- In the US, 5–22% of population has cholelithiasis
- Can lead to:
  - Biliary colic
  - Acute cholecystitis
  - Gallstone pancreatitis
  - Choledocholithiasis
- Majority of patients with cholelithiasis remain asymptomatic

---

## Indications: Asymptomatic Cholelithiasis

- Prophylactic cholecystectomy typically not warranted
- Exceptions:
  - Sickle cell anemia (hepatic and vaso-occlusive disease can mimic acute cholecystitis)
- Other specific patient populations may benefit

---

## Indications: Gallbladder Polyps

- Without cholelithiasis
- Resection recommended for:
  - Polyps ≥10 mm
  - Any size polyp with biliary symptoms
- See Chapter 49 for details

---

## Indications: Concomitant Procedures

- Often performed with:
  - Pancreaticoduodenectomy
  - Major anatomic liver resections
- At time of bariatric surgery – controversial
  - Biliary symptoms may increase after extreme weight loss
  - Meta-analysis: concomitant cholecystectomy increases morbidity and operative time

---

## Indications: Timing of Cholecystectomy

- Varies by indication
- Acute cholecystitis: proceed to OR as early as possible
- Swedish registry study: adverse events, mortality, and CBDIs higher if >4 days after admission
- Optimal timing: within 48 hours of admission for acute cholecystitis

---

## Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy: Introduction

- Standard access for gallbladder removal
- Multiple studies show:
  - Decreased postoperative pain
  - Earlier return to normal activity
  - Decreased hospital length of stay (LOS)
  - Reduction in incisional hernia development
- Familiarity with porta hepatis anatomy reduces complication rates

---

## Operating Room Setup

- Ensure all equipment is present and functional
- Equipment for potentially necessary procedures:
  - Cholangiography
  - Conversion to laparotomy
- See Box 36.1 for full equipment list

---

## Box 36.1: Equipment for Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy – Viewing

- Camera light source
- Laparoscope (5‑mm and 10‑mm, 30°)
- Monitors (one over each shoulder)
- Insufflator and tubing
- Trocars (multiple 5‑mm, at least one 10‑mm)

---

## Box 36.1: Dissection and Removal Instruments

- Clips (5‑mm and 10‑mm varieties)
- Electrocautery
- Suction/irrigation
- Atraumatic graspers
- Maryland grasper (or right‑angle)
- Endoscopic retrieval bag

---

## Box 36.1: Instruments for Unusual Circumstances

- Endoloop
- Laparoscopic needle driver
- Absorbable hemostatic agent
- Staplers
- Argon laser
- Cholangiography equipment (catheter, contrast, C‑arm)
- Open cholecystectomy tray and instruments

---

## Port Placement and Exposure

- After pneumoperitoneum:
  - 5‑ or 10‑mm port in periumbilical region
  - 30° laparoscope inserted, inspect cavity
- Additional ports:
  - Right anterior axillary line, 2 cm below costal margin (5‑mm)
  - Midclavicular line at liver edge (5‑mm)
  - Subxiphoid region, 2–4 cm below xiphoid (5‑ or 10‑mm)
- Optional fifth port for additional retraction

---

## Figure 36.1: Port Positions

- A: Laparoscope (periumbilical)
- B: Grasper for retraction (RUQ subcostal)
- C: Grasper for manipulation (RUQ subcostal)
- D: Subxiphoid for dissector, diathermy, clip appliers
*(See original figure for detailed placement)*

---

## Dissection and Critical View of Safety (CVS)

- Atraumatic grasper through lateral port to retract fundus cephalad and laterally
- Second grasper through midclavicular port to manipulate infundibulum
- Adhesions taken down
- Retract infundibulum caudally and to the right to expose Triangle of Calot

---

## Triangle of Calot – Figure 36.2A

- Limited by:
  - Common hepatic duct
  - Right hepatic duct
  - Cystic duct
  - Inferior liver edge
- This is the cholecystectomy triangle in early descriptions

---

## Triangle of Calot – Figure 36.2B

- Modern definition limited by:
  - Common hepatic duct
  - Cystic duct
  - Cystic artery
- Important for identifying the cystic artery and duct

---

## Opening the Peritoneum

- Cautery instrument through xiphoid port opens peritoneum in Triangle of Calot
- Start at edge of gallbladder neck to avoid iatrogenic injury
- Continue dissection on both sides of gallbladder, 1–2 mm from liver edge

---

## Critical View of Safety (CVS) – Concept

- Technique shown to reduce iatrogenic bile duct injuries
- Recommended by multisociety consensus statement
- If CVS not attainable, perform subtotal cholecystectomy (not fundus‑first approach)
- See Chapters 32 and 42

---

## Achieving CVS – Dissection Steps

- Blunt and cautery dissection of attachments at gallbladder neck
- Serially retract infundibulum medially and laterally
- Avoid dissecting down to common bile duct
- Blunt dissection with Maryland or right‑angle grasper to create window behind cystic duct
- Gallbladder dissected off liver edge, exposing cystic plate

---

## Criteria for CVS – Box 36.2

1. Only two structures seen entering the gallbladder: cystic duct and cystic artery.
2. The lower one‑third of the cystic plate is exposed.
3. Tissue cleared from hepatocystic triangle so structures identified anteriorly and posteriorly.

---

## Box 36.2: Doublet Scoring

- **Two structures connected to gallbladder:** Only two structures clearly seen entering the gallbladder.
- **Cystic plate:** Approximately 1/3 of cystic plate clearly visible.
- **Clearance of hepatocystic triangle:** Cleared of tissue so visibility is unimpeded; surgeon certain no other structures are present.

---

## Figure 36.3A: Critical View – Schematic

- Hepatocystic triangle dissected free of all tissue except cystic duct and artery
- One‑third of cystic plate on liver bed exposed
- When achieved, the two structures entering gallbladder can only be the cystic duct and artery

---

## Figure 36.3B: Critical View – Laparoscopic Image

- Actual intraoperative view demonstrating the CVS
- Only cystic duct and artery entering gallbladder
- Cystic plate clearly visible
- Hepatocystic triangle cleared

---

## CVS in Practice

- Most surgeons attempt CVS, but rarely achieved in practice
- Evaluation of 160 online videos: only one video had passing CVS score
- Safe Cholecystectomy Curriculum available at SAGES website

---

## Completion of Cholecystectomy – Clipping

- Once anatomy confirmed, clip cystic artery and duct
- Avoid tenting CBD with clips placed too distally
- Visualize clip tips to be free before closing
- If clip not possible, use Endoloop
- Scissors divide the structures
- In large inflamed ducts, endovascular staplers may be used (but raise concern for CBD injury)

---

## Completion – Gallbladder Dissection

- Dissect gallbladder off cystic plate from infundibulum to fundus with electrocautery
- Avoid blind clipping, clamping, or cauterizing (risk of hemorrhage or injury)
- Use gallbladder for retraction to inspect hemostasis and clip security

---

## Completion – Specimen Removal

- Removal through periumbilical incision (easily enlarged)
- Use bag extraction with videoscopic visualization to avoid bag rupture
- Spilled bile/debris should be irrigated and cleared
- Fascia of port sites >10 mm closed to prevent hernias (some surgeons omit epigastric closure)

---

## Figure 36.4: Blind Clipping Hazard

- Blind placement of clips or clamps for hemostasis can injure hepatic artery or bile duct.
- Always visualize structures clearly.

---

## Three‑Port and Two‑Port Techniques

- Attempts to reduce number of ports
- Small series suggest feasibility and safety
- Proponents cite reduced cost, fewer scars
- Typically eliminate RUQ ports by using sutures to retract gallbladder

---

## Comparison: Four‑Port vs. Three‑Port

- RCT of 217 patients: no difference in operation length or morbidity (including bile duct injuries)
- No difference in pain medication required
- No obvious advantages over four‑port technique currently

---

## Single‑Incision Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy (SILC)

- Performed through single transabdominal incision (usually umbilicus)
- Special single‑port systems available (FDA‑approved)
- RCTs: longer operating time, higher conversion rate compared to three‑port
- Only advantage: aesthetic score
- More stress on surgeon (higher heart rate, cortisol levels)

---

## SILC – Surgeon Stress

- Double‑blind RCT measured heart rate and salivary cortisol
- SILC associated with higher heart rates and cortisol levels
- Surgeons reported more demanding workload
- CVS must be obtained regardless of number of ports

---

## Robotic‑Assisted Laparoscopic Cholecystectomy

- Increased use due to:
  - Aggressive marketing and patient demand
  - 3D visualization, improved ergonomics, easier learning curve
- Proposed as ideal tool to improve robotic skills

---

## Robotic vs. Laparoscopic – Costs

- Similar outcomes but higher costs:
  - Console ~$2 million
  - Maintenance and disposable instruments expensive
- Single institution: lower readmission rates but higher costs and longer operative time
- Cost discrepancies must be considered

---

## Contraindications – Absolute

- Refractory coagulopathy
- Intolerance of general anesthesia
- 2018 Tokyo Guidelines: Grade III cholecystitis (severe sepsis, end‑organ failure) not a contraindication if supportive care available and patient can withstand procedure

---

## Contraindications – Relative

- Severe cardiopulmonary disease
- Pregnancy
- Cirrhosis with portal hypertension
- Decision based on clinical judgment

---

## Cirrhosis and Cholecystectomy

- Laparoscopic cholecystectomy challenging in cirrhotics:
  - Stiff, friable liver
  - Coagulopathy
  - Aberrant portosystemic collaterals
- Childs‑Pugh A/B: similar outcomes except longer operative time and trend to higher conversion rate
- Feasible even with portal hypertension
- Energy‑sealing device recommended; hemostatic agents and argon beam available
- Convert for significant bleeding

---

## Conversion to Open

- Sometimes necessary
- Conversion rates: 5–15%
- Decision depends on surgeon experience, comfort, patient factors
- Reasons: unclear anatomy, intraoperative complication, failure to progress, pathology not amenable to laparoscopy/endoscopy

---

## Factors Associated with Conversion

- Prior upper abdominal surgery
- Pericholecystic fluid
- Acute cholecystitis
- Emergent cholecystectomy
- Conversion should not be viewed as a complication but as mature judgment to prevent disastrous complications

---

## Open Technique – Incision

- Right subcostal (Kocher) incision
- 2 cm below right costal margin
- Extends from midline to lateral edge of right rectus muscle
- Can be extended superiorly along midline for more exposure

---

## Open Technique – Retrograde Cholecystectomy

- Also requires CVS
- Magnification not available; different exposure
- Principles same to prevent biliary injury
- Fundus grasped, peritoneum over infundibulum incised
- Stay close to gallbladder edge

---

## Retrograde – Cystic Duct Identification

- Suture ligature passed around cystic duct for tension and to prevent stone migration
- Achieve CVS: clear hepatocystic triangle, only two structures entering gallbladder, one‑third cystic plate visible
- Milk stones back into gallbladder
- Ligate cystic artery (clips or sutures) and divide

---

## Retrograde – Cholangiography

- If indicated, perform at this time
- Then ligate and divide cystic duct
- Dissect gallbladder off cystic plate using cautery, staying close to gallbladder
- Avoid entering cystic plate and deeper liver parenchyma

---

## Retrograde – Bleeding from Liver Bed

- Brisk bleeding usually venous (from middle hepatic vein branches)
- Treat with constant pressure for 5–10 minutes
- Hemostatic agents may help
- If fails, deep hemostatic sutures – but be aware of right portal pedicle location

---

## Antegrade (Fundus‑Down) Cholecystectomy

- Alternate technique; not for severe inflammation obscuring cystic duct
- Risk of biliary injury without proper visualization
- Fundus grasped, countertraction on liver edge peritoneum
- Incise gallbladder serosa 5 mm from liver edge

---

## Antegrade – Dissection

- Develop plane between gallbladder wall and cystic plate
- Avoid entering cystic plate
- Extend plane medially and laterally toward neck
- Energy‑sealing device on edematous peritoneum
- Dissect posterior and lateral to free gallbladder

---

## Antegrade – Cystic Artery and Duct

- Exposes cystic artery and duct
- Ligate and transect cystic artery as it enters gallbladder
- Dissect infundibulum to expose cystic duct – do not dissect more than 1 cm (risk of CBD injury)
- Ligate and divide cystic duct, remove gallbladder, close abdomen

---

## Subtotal Cholecystectomy – Indications

- Recommended for severely inflamed gallbladders when CVS cannot be safely obtained
- Fibrosis can shorten cystic duct, fuse with CBD, leading to misidentification
- Avoid dissection in hepatocystic triangle; manage cholecystitis safely
- Partial or subtotal: remove anterior wall, leave posterior wall in place

---

## Subtotal – Technique (Figure 36.6)

- Dissect above the "line of safety" between sulcus of Rouviere and hilar plate
- Drain and open gallbladder at fundus with cautery
- Suction bile/stones; place in specimen bag
- Extend incision to gallbladder neck without dissecting cystic duct/artery
- Remove anterior wall completely, leave posterior wall on cystic plate

---

## Subtotal – Remnant Management

- Coagulate remnant mucosa with cautery or argon beam
- Place drain near gallbladder stump
- Performed both open and laparoscopically
- Higher risk of bile leaks and subphrenic collection (up to 3‑fold relative risk)
- Leaks more common if remnant left open

---

## Figure 36.5: Mistaking Common Hepatic Duct

- In severe inflammation, the common hepatic duct can be mistaken for cystic duct
- This leads to classic injury
- Always be cautious

---

## Figure 36.6: Line of Safety

- Line between sulcus of Rouviere and hilar plate
- Ensures dissection away from CBD in severe inflammation
- Proximal limit for subtotal cholecystectomy

---

## Figure 36.7A–B: Subtotal Cholecystectomy

- A: Laparoscopic subtotal – anterior wall excised, posterior wall left attached to liver
- B: Open subtotal – similar approach
- Remnant mucosa can be removed or coagulated

---

## Anatomic Variations – Introduction

- Essential to know biliary anatomy and variations
- Rare gallbladder variations (duplicated, left‑sided, bilobed, absent) – usually identified preoperatively
- Focus on biliary variations that can lead to injury

---

## Cystic Duct Junction Variations (Figure 36.8)

- Cystic duct and hepatic duct junction vary
- Common hepatic duct length 1–7.5 cm
- MRI study: 40.7% had some biliary variant
- 5% had medial cystic duct insertion

---

## Figure 36.8: Cystic Duct Variations

- A: Various confluence patterns
- B: High insertion of cystic duct (demonstrated on ERCP)

---

## Anomalous Extrahepatic Bile Ducts

- Occur in up to 12% of patients
- Most common: anomalous right sectoral duct emptying into common hepatic or cystic duct
- Often represents only biliary drainage for corresponding liver segment
- Injury causes atrophy or obstructive cholangitis

---

## Figure 36.9: Variations of Right Sectoral Ducts

- A: Variations in confluence of extrahepatic bile ducts and cystic duct
- B: Cholangiogram showing cystic duct inserting into right anterior section bile duct

---

## Arterial Anatomic Variations

- Cystic artery origin: right hepatic artery (76%), but may branch from left, common, or proper hepatic arteries
- Arterial injury may accompany bile duct injury (vasculobiliary injury)
- Right hepatic artery involved in 92% of combined injuries due to proximity to CBD

---

## Postoperative Management

- Elective laparoscopic: same‑day discharge
- Acute cholecystitis: often overnight observation
- Elderly, comorbid, significant analgesia, complicated procedures may benefit from admission
- Diet allowed shortly after surgery
- Pain: oral narcotics, but many manage with NSAIDs and acetaminophen
- Follow‑up: 1–4 weeks

---

## Immediate Complications: Biliary Injury – Overview

- Most feared complication
- 30‑day mortality ~2% in large database
- Mean survival after injury: 17.6 years; worse physical QoL, loss of productivity; 34.9% receive disability benefits
- Incidence: 0.08–0.25%

---

## Biliary Injury – Role of Intraoperative Cholangiography

- Proposed to reduce injury; but retrospective studies show higher incidence when performed (0.25% vs. 0.12%) – likely because used more in challenging cases
- Proper identification and interpretation needed
- CVS remains standard to reduce injury

---

## Biliary Injury – Risk Factors

- Inflammation increases risk
- Severity of cholecystitis correlates with CBDI risk
- "Classic injury" – CBD mistaken for cystic duct, ligated
- Occurs when gallbladder retracted too aggressively to the right, causing cystic duct to lie parallel to CBD

---

## Figure 36.10: Pathogenesis of Classic Injury

1. CBD mistaken as cystic duct, clipped and divided.
2. Dissection carried up along left side of common hepatic duct (thinking it's underside of gallbladder).
3. Common hepatic duct transected while attempting to dissect gallbladder; often right hepatic artery injured.
(From Strasberg SM, Helton WS.)

---

## Biliary Injury – Intraoperative Management

- Assess extent, own experience, patient condition, hospital resources
- Call hepatobiliary surgeon if available
- If specialist not available: place drain near porta, close, transfer
- Avoid proceeding with gallbladder extraction after identifying injury (risk of amplifying injury)

---

## Biliary Injury – Postoperative Detection

- Not always discovered intraoperatively
- Ongoing pain, fevers, ileus should raise suspicion
- Initial: abdominal ultrasound, then CT
- Excessive fluid: percutaneous drainage
- Determine injury type with MRCP, PTC, ERCP
- Simple leaks: drainage ± ERCP stenting
- Complex injuries: percutaneous‑endoscopic rendezvous procedures in specialized centers

---

## Bleeding – Incidence and Sources

- Clinically significant bleeding: 0.1–1.9%
- Sources:
  1. Liver bed (terminal branches of middle hepatic vein)
  2. Abdominal arterial source
  3. Port sites
- Liver bed bleeding (venous) – control with hemostatic agents and pressure, increase pneumoperitoneum

---

## Bleeding – Management

- Clips or sutures in cystic plate if landmarks identified
- If visualization lost: apply pressure, convert to laparotomy
- During laparotomy, maintain pressure on venous injury to prevent air embolus
- Acute hemodynamic decline postoperatively: consider bleeding from dislodged clip

---

## Retained Common Bile Duct Stones – Prevalence

- Present in 5–15% of patients undergoing cholecystectomy
- Suspected choledocholithiasis: preoperative MRCP or ERCP recommended
- Laparoscopic CBD exploration reduces LOS and cost vs. endoscopic + cholecystectomy

---

## Retained Stones – Postoperative Incidence

- Rare: ~1.8% incidence of postoperative ERCP for suspected retained stones
- Suspected: MRCP or ERCP
- Endoscopic sphincteroplasty with stone extraction is standard treatment

---

## Gallbladder Perforation

- Common during procedure, especially early in learning curve
- Careful retraction essential
- Spillage of bile and stones can lead to:
  - Abscess
  - Fistula formation
- In incidental gallbladder carcinoma: bile spillage increases carcinomatosis (24% vs. 4%) and worsens disease‑free survival

---

## Delayed Complications: Remnant Gallbladder and Cystic Duct Stones

- Rare; recurrent stones in remnant or cystic duct
- Presents with pain similar to pre‑cholecystectomy symptoms
- Can occur 4 months to 25 years later
- Usually associated with subtotal cholecystectomy

---

## Diagnosis and Treatment of Remnant Stones

- Diagnosis: MRCP, ERCP, EUS, intraoperative cholangiogram, PTC
- Treatment:
  - Endoscopic retrieval or lithotripsy
  - Surgical extraction and ligation closer to common duct
  - Completion cholecystectomy (open or laparoscopic) – low morbidity

---

## Biliary Strictures – Incidence

- Benign strictures occur in up to 2.7% of laparoscopic and 0.5% of open cholecystectomies
- Causes: incomplete transection, clipping/ligation, thermal injury, ischemic devascularization
- Presentation: obstructive jaundice

---

## Management of Biliary Strictures

- Endoscopic stenting first – 67% symptom‑free at 28 months
- Normal ERCP after stenting predicts no stricture recurrence
- Surgery remains mainstay for non‑responders – 84% long‑term patency in meta‑analysis

---

## Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea

- Defined as ≥3 loose stools per day after cholecystectomy
- Prevalence difficult to assess
- Multifactorial: increased bile salts in colon causing secretory diarrhea
- Altered gut microbiome (higher Proteobacteria) in patients with diarrhea

---

## Treatment of Postcholecystectomy Diarrhea

- Bile‑acid binding agents
- Antidiarrheals
- Variable results

---

## Conclusion

- Cholecystectomy is gold standard for gallbladder disease
- Majority performed minimally invasively with excellent results
- Now often ambulatory
- Continuous drive to improve outcomes and reduce CBDIs
- Education on CVS and when to pursue subtotal cholecystectomy is key
- Safety of patient remains paramount alongside innovation
